ABSTRACT
Ultra-small nanoparticles, nanowires, and two-dimensional nanosheets have attracted much attention in acute kidney injury
(AKI) treatment. However, the influence of nanostructure geometry on AKI therapy remains unknown. It is important to
investigate their biodistribution, clearance, and toxicology to identify the most potential geometry for further nanomedical
applications. Herein, three types of oxygen-deficient tungsten oxide (WOx) nanostructures, nanodots, nanowires, and nanosheets,
with attractive reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging and computed tomography (CT) imaging properties are bottom-up
synthesized, and their in vivo behaviors are systematically studied. The biodistribution results demonstrate that all three WOx
nanostructures can penetrate from the kidney and excrete to the bladder. Interestingly, nanodots can accumulate and be cleared
quickly from the kidney, while nanosheets have long retention in vivo. In marked contrast to nanodots and nanosheets, nanowires
show high levels in the lung organs with significant cytotoxicity. Therapeutic experiments suggest that nanodots and nanosheets
have better therapeutic effects on AKI, but the therapeutic effect of nanowires is not obvious. Furthermore, the nanosheets
perform better in alleviating AKI at a lower injection dose than nanodots. This work demonstrates that nanosheets, among various
geometries, have particular potential for further AKI treatment because of outstanding performance in CT imaging, renal targeting,
long-time retention, and low toxicity. The “structure-function” correlations enable the reasonable design of nanoprobes for AKI
theragnostic.

Introduction
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common clinical complication,
which is associated with poor outcomes such as chronic kidney
disease, end-stage renal disease, and even mortality [1, 2]. AKI
refers to abnormal renal function characterized by a sudden
decline in glomerular filtration rate, which leads to the increased
accumulation of nitrogen metabolism in the blood. Although
the pathogenesis of AKI is complex, it is widely accepted that
oxidative stress plays an important role in AKI development.
The excessive ROS generated by dysfunctional mitochondria can
induce oxidative stress by reacting with cellular biomolecules,
subsequently causing renal injury. Therefore, ROS scavenging
strategies based on antioxidant drugs hold significant potential
in the prevention and treatment of AKI [3]. For example, the
antioxidant N-acetyl cysteine (NAC) has been proven to prevent
AKI development. However, their clinical applications are limited
by low stability, poor water solubility, and unsatisfied kidney
targeting properties.
The burgeoning field of nanotechnology demonstrates significant
translational potential in biomedical applications, particularly
in targeted drug delivery [4–7] and diagnostic imaging [8–10]
that enables highly effective therapeutic effects [11]. Within the
context of AKI therapeutics research, advances in nanotech-
nology have enabled the development of various functional
nanostructures with antioxidant properties to scavenge ROS [12].
Nevertheless, not all of them can be applied in AKI therapy
because of the renal filtration threshold. The glomerular filtration
membrane comprises three layers [13–15]. The first inner layer
is fenestrated endothelium with anionic glycoproteins and 70–
90 nm pores. The second intermediate layer is a basement
membrane containing heparan sulfate proteoglycans, collagen IV,
and laminin, acting as dual mechanical/charge barriers. The third
outer layer is podocyte foot processes forming 4–11 nm slit pores.
Besides that, nanostructures exceeding renal filtration thresholds
predominantly undergo rapid uptake by the reticuloendothelial
system due to nonspecific phagocytic recognition triggered by
their large hydrodynamic dimensions [16]. Thus, the size- and
charge-dependent filtration governs renal targeting of engineered
nanomaterials [17–19].
Ultra-small nanoparticles, nanowires, and two-dimensional (2D)
nanosheets have attracted great attention in the imaging and
treatment of AKI [20]. (1) Ultra-small nanoparticles with a
hydrodynamic size of less than 10 nm have been demonstrated
to evade capture by the mononuclear phagocyte system and
are excreted by the glomerulus [21]. Up to now, ultra-small
antioxidant nanoparticles such as polyoxometalate clusters, redox
polymer [22–25], ceria [26, 27], and so on exhibit high stability,
broad-spectrum ROS elimination activities, and rapid renal clear-
ance, enabling great potential in AKI management [28–35]. (2)
The interaction of both multi-walled carbon nanotubes or single-
walled carbon nanotubes with the biological milieu has also
been investigated [36]. Evidence shows that carbon nanotubes
can rapidly permeate through glomerular pores and excrete into
the urinary [37, 38], which can be used as carriers to deliver
siRNA for the therapy of AKI. (3) Some 2D nanosheets also
display attractive chemical reactivity toward ROS and high rates
of accumulation in the kidneys. For example, black phospho-
rus nanosheets [39], rectangular DNA origami nanostructure
[40–42], and 2D Ti3C2 MXene [43] have been explored as
therapeutic agents for AKI treatment. It is critically imperative
to investigate the influence of their geometry on biodistribu-
tion, clearance, and toxicology, and finally to identify which
geometry of nanostructure agents is the most promising in AKI
treatment.
Given the strong X-ray attenuation of tungsten, the biodis-
tribution of tungsten-based nanostructures can be explored
by CT imaging with high time-spatial resolutions [44]. CT
imaging is currently one of the most powerful imaging tools
for clinical diagnosis, which are non-invasive, and can afford
three-dimensional (3D) images of whole-body structures [45].
On the other hand, WOx nanostructures hold an intrinsic
characteristic of ROS-responsive biodegradability. Such property
makes it an attractive candidate with fast clearance and reduced
toxicity.
Taking the advantage of WOx nanostructure in biomedicine, we
herein synthesized three representative WOx nanostructures with
ROS scavenging ability, namely that of nanodots, nanowires, and
nanosheets, to explore the effect of geometry on renal targeting
ability and treatment performance (Scheme 1). First, the physico-
chemical properties were characterized to confirm the formation
of three geometries of WOx nanostructures. Second, the ROS
scavenging ability was also tested in vitro. Next, CT imaging
and inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectrometry
(ICP-AES) were used to explore their biodistributions and renal-
targeting properties. Finally, the relationship between injection
doses and AKI therapeutic effects was investigated through blood
biochemistry and histology analysis.
2
Results and Discussion
2.1
Synthesis and Characterization of WOx
Nanodots, WOx Nanowires, and WOx Nanosheets
Nanodots, nanowires, and nanosheets were synthesized accord-
ing to previously reported methods with little modifications
[46, 47]. Transmission electron microscope (TEM) images in
Figure 1a–c displayed uniform nanodots with a diameter of about
5.7 nm, nanowires with a length of about 80.2 nm, and rectangular
nanosheets with an edge length of 142.5 nm, respectively. X-ray
diffraction (XRD) in Figure 1d–f was further used to confirm those
nanostructures and the results indicated the successful synthesis
of nanodots, nanowires, and nanosheets. The surface chemistry
of these nanostructures was analyzed by X-ray photoelectron
spectroscopy (XPS), as illustrated in Figures 1g–i and S1. The
peaks at 35.44 eV and 37.57 eV represent the W 4f7/2 and W 4f5/2
states of W6+, while the peaks at 33.93 eV and 36.00 eV correspond
with the W 4f7/2 and W 4f5/2 states of W5+. Figure 1j shows
the average hydrodynamic diameters of nanodots, nanowires,
and nanosheets revealed by dynamic light scattering (DLS) are
10.1 nm, 91.3 nm, and 190.1 nm, respectively. It is obvious
that the hydrodynamic sizes of nanosheets and nanowires are
above the kidney filtration threshold. DLS characterization in
Figure 1k also reveals that nanodots, nanowires, and nanosheets
possess negative zeta potentials of –31.2 mV, –26.2 mV, and –
45.3 mV, respectively. UV-vis-NIR spectra in Figure 1l show these

2.2
ROS Elimination Abilities of WOx Nanodots,
WOx Nanowires, and WOx Nanosheets
Representative ROS, H2O2, was chosen to explore the ROS scav-
enging ability of those nanostructures. As shown in Figure 2a–c,
all the nanostructures exhibited strong H2O2 elimination ability.
The blue color of nanodots and nanowires gradually disap-
peared with the increment of H2O2 concentration from 0 mM
to 10 mM, which was attributed to the oxidation of W5+ by
H2O2 (Figure 2a,b). Consequently, their NIR absorptions were
decreased (Figure 2d,e). Notably, it seemed that the color of
nanosheets did not change at all in the presence of H2O2
(Figure 2c). Nevertheless, the NIR absorption decreased gradually
upon the addition of H2O2 (Figure 2f). Although all three types
of WOx nanostructures were sensitive to H2O2, Figure 2g–i
shows that in the presence of 2 mM of H2O2, 17% of nan-
odots, 53% of nanowires, and 62% of nanosheets are oxidized,
respectively, indicating WOx nanosheets perform best in H2O2
scavenging. The oxidization of W5+ to W6+ endowed these WOx
nanostructures with sensitive H2O2-responsive abilities, which
was proved by XPS (Figure 2j–l). Further, their antioxidant
properties toward free radicals were also investigated by the 2,2′-
azino-bis (3-ethylbenzothiazoline 6-sulfonate) (ABTS) radical
assay. As shown in Figure 2m–o, 40 µg/mL of nanodots can
scavenge approximately 14% of the free radicals, 40 µg/mL of
nanowires can eliminate 29% of the free radicals, while 40
µg/mL of nanosheets can decompose 51% of the free radicals.
Taken together, nanosheets performed best in ROS scavenging
in vitro.
The differences in ROS scavenging capacity among the three WOx
nanostructures can be attributed to their structural variations
because they contain the same tungsten concentration. Com-
pared to WOx nanodots and WOx nanowires, WOx nanosheets
exhibit significant advantages due to their unique properties,
including an ultra-thin layer structure, large specific surface
area, and distinctive kidney-targeting ability. Most atoms in
nanosheets are directly exposed on their surfaces, endowing these
materials with the largest specific surface area and extraordinary
surface activity [48]. They can act as antioxidants with maximum

2.3
In Vivo Biodistribution of WOx
Nanostructures With Different Geometry
Inspired by the good performance in the ROS elimination, Cell
counting kit-8 (CCK-8) assay was performed to evaluate whether
these WOx nanostructures can lead to potential cytotoxicity on
normal mice. Figure S2 shows human embryonic kidney 293T
(HEK-293T) cells treated by nanodots, nanowires, or nanosheets,
display negligible cytotoxicity. The impacts of these nanostruc-
tures on blood chemistry and organ histopathology were also
evaluated on normal mice to investigate their biocompatibility.
As shown in Figure S3, no necrosis is observed in the liver,
heart, spleen, lung, and kidney at 14 days after intravenous
injection of nanodots, nanowires, or nanosheets at a dose of 10
mg/kg, respectively. Moreover, the results of blood biochemical
analysis show no obvious differences between the normal and
nanostructure-treated groups, indicating no obvious toxicity of
these nanostructures (Figure S4). Therefore, it is reasonable to
conclude that those nanostructures have good biocompatibility
in normal mice.

AKI mice via ICP-AES. The AKI mice model was successfully
established through intraperitoneal injection of 20 mg/kg of cis-
platinum into normal mice (Figure S5). 48 h after induction of

2.4
Dynamic CT Imaging of AKI Mice Treated by
WOx Nanodots, WOx Nanowires, or WOx Nanosheets
Taking advantage of strong X-ray attenuation characterization,
tungsten-based nanostructures could act as CT contrast agents
[49]. CT imaging is widely used in the clinic for medical diagnosis,
by which the 3D structure of the whole body with high resolution,
real-time monitoring, and noninvasive could be obtained. To
further uncover the biodistribution of WOx nanostructures with
different geometries, we evaluated the feasibility of these nanos-
tructures as CT contrast agents by using various concentrations of
nanodots, nanowires, and nanosheets to require X-ray phantom
images, respectively. As we can see from Figure 3d,e, for all
types of nanostructures, the signals of X-ray CT images become
gradually stronger with increasing concentrations. The slope of
the HU value for those nanostructures were 54 HU L/g, 60 HU
L/g, and 72 HU L/g, suggesting the attractive contrast efficacy of
these nanostructures for CT imaging. It should be noted that CT
absorption coefficient of the nanosheet was higher than that of
the others, which indicated the potential of the nanosheet as a
best CT contrast agent among those geometries.
Next, CT imaging was used to investigate renal targeting and
clearance properties of these nanostructures. After intravenous
injection, CT scans at 10 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 4 h,
5 h, and 6 h from the kidneys and bladders were performed
to monitor the behavior of these nanostructures in AKI mice,
respectively, as shown in Figure 4. It should be noted that
nanowires were more likely to cause the death of AKI mice,
thus the injection dose of nanowires was halved compared to
nanodots and nanosheets. Strong CT signals were immediately
observed in the bladders after injection of nanodots, nanowires,
and nanosheets, respectively (Figure 4a–i), whereas no CT signals
could be detected without the injection of WOx nanostructures
(Figure S6), indicating that these nanostructures were all prone
to penetrating glomeruli from AKI mice. The results illustrated
in Figure 4a–c show that nanodots can be cleared at 3 h
post-injection. However, there was still obviously increased CT
signal in the bladder of nanosheet-treated mice after 5 h post-
injection, indicating the long retention time of nanosheet, as
given in Figure 4g–i. Therefore, CT results indicated that all
three nanostructures could target and be eliminated from the
kidney, nanowires had high cytotoxicity, nanodots could be
cleared quickly from the kidney whereas nanosheets had a long
retention time, which was consistent with the results of in vivo
biodistribution measured by ICP-AES.

In addition, to further understand the physiological mechanism
of WOx nanosheets against AKI, we measured the antioxidant
activity in renal tissues. Compared with AKI mice, the AKI
mice treated with WOx nanosheets exhibited a remarkably
decreased malondialdehyde (MDA) level (Figure S7a). Further-
more, superoxide dismutase (SOD) and glutathione peroxidase
(GPx) activities in AKI mice reduced significantly, while the
activities of SOD and GPx in the kidneys of AKI mice treated
with WOx nanosheets were similar to normal mice (Figure S7b,c).
Kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1) is an important biomarker
of kidney injury. The AKI mice treated with WOx nanosheets
showed a significantly decreased level of KIM-1 (Figure S7f), fur-
ther demonstrating the therapeutic effect. In addition, to evaluate
the anti-inflammatory effect of WOx nanosheets, we measured
the levels of key inflammatory factors, including interleukin-6
(IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), using enzyme-linked
immunosorbent assay (ELISA). As shown in Figure S7d,e, WOx
nanosheets significantly inhibited the inflammatory cytokines in
damaged kidneys. These results demonstrated the high therapeu-
tic effect of WOx nanosheets in alleviating AKI.
Oxidative stress plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of
AKI. Excessive ROS can damage kidney cells and tissues, ulti-
mately resulting in inflammation and apoptosis. The W5+ in
WOx nanostructures possess strong reducing properties, making
them effective for scavenging ROS, ultimately inhibiting fur-
ther kidney damage. Thus, the ROS scavenging ability and the
kidney accumulation property of these nanostructures are two
key factors influencing the therapeutic efficacy. Among these
nanostructures, WOx nanosheets possess a large specific surface
area, enabling them to readily interact with vascular endothelial
cells, increasing their accumulation in the kidneys. Besides that,
our results indicate that nanosheets have a longer retention time
in the injured kidney (Figure 4). The excellent renal targeting
property, long retention time in the injured kidney, and strong
ROS scavenging ability (Figure 2) make WOx nanosheets perform
best in the AKI treatment.

3
Conclusions
Three types of WOx nanostructures, nanodots, nanowires, and
nanosheets, were synthesized to explore the effects of geometry
on in vivo biodistribution and AKI therapy. The characterization,
ROS responsibility, biosafety, renal-targeting property, biodistri-
bution, and therapeutic efficacy of the three WOx nanostructures
had been systemically investigated. Experimental results showed
that tungsten-based nanodots, nanowires, and nanosheets exhib-
ited antioxidant activities toward H2O2 and free radicals. We
also studied their renal-targeting property using CT imaging, and
found that all three nanostructures were prone to elimination
from the mouse body in the urine, suggesting their penetration
ability from the glomerulus and potential treatment for AKI.
During the test for CT imaging, we found the mice treated
with nanowires are very easy to die, indicating the toxicity
of nanowires. The biodistribution result showed an abundant
accumulation of nanowires in lung organs, which may be the
reason for high toxicity. The biodistribution result also disclosed
that nanodots could accumulate in the kidneys quickly and mas-
sively compared to nanosheets. With high ROS-responsive and
renal-targeting properties, nanosheets at lower doses exhibited
therapeutic efficacy for AKI treatment, which had been proved
by BUN and CRE measurement, H&E staining, and TUNEL
staining. In addition, as expected, nanowires showed unsatis-
factory performances in alleviating AKI. The complex etiology
and unclear pathological mechanisms of AKI present significant
challenges for the clinical development of nanomedicines. This
work is the first time to compare the behaviors of three different
geometries of nanostructures in AKI treatment. Our results
demonstrate that nanosheets, among various shapes, are the
most promising candidates to reverse AKI. In conclusion, this
article offers valuable reference for researchers in developing
new nanomedicines for treating AKI, which holds substantial
theoretical and practical significance for the advancement of AKI
drug research.
4
Experimental Section
4.1
General Methods, Reagents, and Supplies
Tungsten hexachloride (≥99.9%, CAS: 13283-01-7) and D-(+)-
Glucose (≥99.5%, CAS: 50-99-7) were purchased from Sigma-
Aldrich. Polyvinylpyrrolidone (MW40000, CAS: 9003-39-8) and
sodium tungstate dehydrate (99%, CAS: 10213-10-2) were obtained
from Innochem (Beijing) Technology Co., Ltd. Acetone (GR, CAS:
67-64-1), hydrochloric acid (GR, CAS: 7647-01-0) and Ethanol
(GR, CAS: 64-17-5) were prepared from Yonghua Chemical
Reagent Co., Ltd. Citric acid monohydrate (>99.5%, CAS: 5949-
29-1) was purchased from Alfa Aesar. CCK-8 assay kit was
obtained from NEST Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Wuxi, China). The
water used in all experiments was ultrapure. All of the chemical
reagents of analytical grade were used as received without further
purification.
Male BALB/C mice (6–8 weeks old) were purchased from
Changzhou Cavins Model Animal Co. Ltd. Approval of exper-
imental procedures on animals was obtained from the Institu-
tional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of Soochow
University. All animal experiments reported herein were carried
out according to the protocols approved by Soochow University
Laboratory Animal Center. The assigned accreditation number of
the investigator is 202404A0113.
4.2
Characterizations
Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEM) images were acquired
by a FEI Technai G2 transmission electron microscope at
an acceleration voltage of 120 kV. The hydrodynamic size
and Zeta potential were measured by Malvern Zetasizer Nano
ZS90. Ultraviolet-visible-near infrared absorption spectrum was
recorded on a Shimadzu UV-Vis-NIR spectrophotometer UV-
3600 using quartz cuvettes with an optical path of 1 cm. Crystal
structure and oxidation state of WOx nanostructures were ana-
lyzed using X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Bruker D8 Advance) with
a scan rate of 0.3 s per step with a step size of 24. X-ray photo-
electron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were operated by an
ESCALAB 250 Xi (Thermo Scientific, America) X-ray resource.
All the binding energies were referred to the C 1s peak at 284.8
eV. Computed Tomography Imaging (CT imaging) was performed
using an animal SPECT with integrated CT system (MILabs,
Utrecht, the Netherlands). The elemental concentrations (i.e., W)
were measured by Inductively Coupled Plasma-Atomic Emission
Spectrometry (ICP-AES).
4.3
Synthesis of WOx Nanodots
WOx nanodots were synthesized by a one-step solvothermal
route. The precursor of WOx nanodots was synthesized in vacuum
glove box to ensure an oxygen-free environment. In a typical
preparation process, WCl6 (50 mg) was dissolved in ethanol
(8 mL) with vigorously stirring until a transparent yellow solution
was formed, followed by adding 8 mL ethanol of 200 mg PVP
(40,000 Da). After continuous stirring for 40 min, the obtained
transparent yellow solution was then transferred to a 25 mL
Teflon-lined autoclave and heated at 200◦C for 1 h. After being
cooled to room temperature, the resulting WOx nanodots were
precipitated by adding acetone, followed by washing with acetone
and ethanol for several times. The product was finally dispersed
in ultrapure water for further use.
4.4
Synthesis of WOx Nanowires
Take the same steps as described above before heating. The
precursor of WOx nanowires was synthesized in vacuum glove
box to ensure an oxygen-free environment. The Teflon-lined
autoclave was heated at 200◦C for 48 h. After being cooled to
room temperature, the resulting WOx nanowires were obtained
and collected by centrifugation, followed by washing with ethanol
and ultrapure water for several times. The product was finally
dispersed in ultrapure water for further use.
4.5
Synthesis of WOx Nanosheets
WOx nanosheets were synthesized by a hydrothermal method.
The precursor of WOx nanosheets was synthesized in the air.
The typical preparation process dissolved 1 mmol Na2WO4⋅2H2O

4.6
XPS Measurement of WOx Nanostructures
XPS measurement of WOx nanostructures was performed before
and after completely oxidized by ROS (i.e., H2O2). Full scans of
the nanostructures were conducted first, then the depth profiles
of spots on the samples were performed. For Ar plasma etching,
we used 3000 eV for 10 s each step, for a total of five steps.
4.7
H2O2 Scavenging Activity of WOx
Nanostructures
The H2O2 scavenging activity of WOx nanostructures was deter-
mined by UV-Vis-NIR spectrophotometry. In brief, a series
of concentration gradient solutions of H2O2 react with WOx
nanostructures. The W concentration of WOx nanostructures
were determined by ICP-AES, which was fixed as 300 µg/mL,
while the concentration of H2O2 was set as 0, 0.1, 1, 2, 5,
and 10 mM, respectively. After 25 min of incubation at room
temperature, photographs were taken to show the color variation
of WOx solutions induced by H2O2. Meanwhile, UV-Vis-NIR
spectra of the reaction mixtures solution were also recorded. The
ultraviolet absorption was detected to measure the clearance rate
of H2O2.
4.8
ABTS Free Radical Scavenging Activity of
WOx Nanostructures
The ABTS free radical scavenging capacity of the samples were
assessed using the total antioxidant capacity assay kit (Yuanye
Biotechnology Co., Ltd, Shanghai, China) according to the
manufacturer’s instructions.
4.9
Cell Culture
HEK-293T cell line was used in this work. Cell medium for HEK-
293T cells was composed of DMEM with 10% fetal bovine serum
(FBS) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin. The cells were maintained
at 37◦C and in 5% CO2 atmosphere.
4.10
CCK-8 Cytotoxicity Assay
Cytotoxicity of WOx nanostructures on HEK-293T cells was tested
by using a standard CCK-8 cytotoxicity assay. Briefly, HEK-293T
cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 1 × 104 cells
per well and incubated at 37◦C under 5% CO2 for 24 h. After the
medium was removed and washed three times with PBS, WOx
nanostructures at the different concentrations (0, 25, 50, 100, 150
µg/mL) in 200 µL of culture medium were added to the wells
and incubated for 24 h. Each concentration was tested in three
replicates as parallel groups. After removing the medium and
washing it with PBS, 20 µL of CCK-8 solution and 180 µL medium
were added to each well and incubated for another 30 min. The
result was measured by the microplate reader.
4.11
Establishment of the AKI Mice Model
Male BALB/C mice (6–8 weeks old, approximately 20 g)
were obtained from Changzhou Cavins Model Animal Co.
Ltd, Changzhou, China. To establish cis-platinum-induced AKI
models, all mice were received intraperitoneal injections of
cis-platinum (20 mg/kg). The mice were euthanized 72 h after cis-
platinum injection. At the meantime, the kidneys were harvested
and then subjected to H&E staining for comparing with those of
normal mice serving as control.
4.12
Biodistribution of WOx Nanostructures
To investigate the biodistribution of WOx nanostructures in the
major organs, male BALB/C mice (n = 3) with established cis-
platinum-induced AKI model were intravenously injected with
WOx nanostructures at a dose of 200 µg. Mice were sacrificed to
harvest major organs including liver, spleen, lung, and kidney and
urine at different time intervals (30 min, 2 h, 6 h). The tissues
were weighed, homogenized, and then dissolved in nitric acid to
calculate the percentage of injected dose per gram of tissue (%
ID/g) by ICP-AES.
4.13
CT Imaging
For in vitro CT imaging, WOx nanostructures were suspended
in aqueous solutions at varying concentrations: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1,
2, and 4 mg/mL. The signal intensities of the region of interest
(ROI) were measured for each sample. In vivo CT imaging
protocol, the AKI mice were anesthetized with isoflurane and
placed in an animal bed. Subsequently, WOx nanostructures were
administered intravenously for CT imaging purposes. Serial CT
scans were conducted at multiple time intervals post-injection
(pre, 10 min, 30 min, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 h. The images were scanned
in the normal mode using full angle, 1 frame averaging, 615
mA tube current, and 60 kV tube voltage. The software package
provided by MILabs reconstructed the final CT images and then
analyzed using PMOD software.
4.14
Investigation of AKI Therapeutic Effects by
WOx Nanostructures

group 1 was healthy mice treated with PBS; group 2 was AKI
mice treated with PBS; group 3 was AKI mice treated with 0.1

AKI model induction; group 4 was AKI mice treated with 0.1

4.16
Biocompatibility Assays
To evaluate the impact of WOx nanostructures on healthy mice,
a regimen of three intravenous injections, each delivering 200 µg
of the nanostructures, was administered over three consecutive
days. Each experimental group consisted of five mice, ensuring a
robust dataset for analysis. On day 14 post-treatment initiation,
blood samples were meticulously collected from the animals.
Following this, the mice were humanely euthanized. Their major
organs, encompassing the heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney,
were carefully excised and then fixed in a 4% paraformaldehyde
solution for H&E staining.
4.17
Analysis of Renal Tissues After WOx
Nanosheets Treatment
The kidneys of mice were frozen and stored at –80◦C. Kidney
homogenates were prepared according to the protocols of dif-
ferent assays. MDA, SOD, and GPx level were assessed with
corresponding assay kits obtained from Beyotime. IL-6 and TNF-
α and KIM-1 expression were measured with related ELISA kits
purchased from mlbio.

Abstract: Ultra-small nanoparticles, nanowires, and two-dimensional nanosheets have attracted much attention in acute kidney injury (AKI) treatment. However, the influence of nanostructure geometry on AKI therapy remains unknown. It is important to investigate their biodistribution, clearance, and toxicology to identify the most potential geometry for further nanomedical applications. Herein, three types of oxygen-deficient tungsten oxide (WOx) nanostructures, nanodots, nanowires, and nanosheets, with attractive reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging and computed tomography (CT) imaging properties are bottom-up synthesized, and their in vivo behaviors are systematically studied. The biodistribution results demonstrate that all three WOx nanostructures can penetrate from the kidney and excrete to the bladder. Interestingly, nanodots can accumulate and be cleared quickly from the kidney, while nanosheets have long retention in vivo. In marked contrast to nanodots and nanosheets, nanowires show high levels in the lung organs with significant cytotoxicity. Therapeutic experiments suggest that nanodots and nanosheets have better therapeutic effects on AKI, but the therapeutic effect of nanowires is not obvious. Furthermore, the nanosheets perform better in alleviating AKI at a lower injection dose than nanodots. This work demonstrates that nanosheets, among various geometries, have particular potential for further AKI treatment because of outstanding performance in CT imaging, renal targeting, long-time retention, and low toxicity. The “structure-function” correlations enable the reasonable design of nanoprobes for AKI theragnostic. Yi Wang and Yueping Li contributed equally to this work.
